_how_to_edit: One entry per page, keyed by the page's address name (slug). 'about' is the short explanation on the element page, 'branches' are the sub-fields shown as chips. Edit freely, then run tools/build_site.py.

organic-chemistry.about: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds: how they are built, how they react, and why their shapes decide what they do. It is the language of medicines, plastics, dyes and most of the molecules of life.

physical-chemistry.about: Physical chemistry explains chemistry with physics: why reactions happen, how fast, and how much energy they move. It turns observations into equations that predict what molecules will do.

analytical-chemistry.about: Analytical chemistry answers two questions: what is in a sample, and how much. It builds the methods and instruments every other field relies on, from drug quality control to environmental monitoring.

theoretical-chemistry.about: Theoretical chemistry describes molecules with mathematics, starting from quantum mechanics. It explains bonding and reactivity from first principles and powers the simulations used across chemistry.

structural-chemistry.about: Structural chemistry determines where every atom sits and why. Knowing a molecule's exact geometry explains its stability, its reactivity and how it packs into crystals.

chemical-kinetics.about: Chemical kinetics measures how fast reactions go and what controls their speed. Rate laws reveal mechanisms, the hidden sequence of steps between reactants and products.

thermochemistry.about: Thermochemistry tracks the heat released or absorbed when chemicals react or change phase. It tells you whether a fuel is worth burning and how much energy a bond really holds.

entropy-in-chemistry.about: Entropy measures how many ways energy and matter can be arranged. Together with enthalpy it decides, through free energy, which reactions run on their own and which never will.

solutions-chemistry.about: Solutions chemistry studies what happens when substances dissolve: solubility, solvation and the equilibria that follow. Most of chemistry, and all of biology, happens in solution.

chemical-structure-and-reactivity.about: This field links a molecule's structure to the way it reacts. Electronic and steric effects explain why one site reacts and another doesn't, and let chemists predict outcomes before running a reaction.

synthetic-chemistry.about: Synthetic chemistry is the craft of making molecules on purpose. It designs routes from simple starting materials to complex targets, and increasingly uses flow reactors and automation to do it faster.

heterocyclic-chemistry.about: Heterocycles are rings that contain atoms other than carbon, usually nitrogen, oxygen or sulfur. They form the core of most drugs, many dyes and the bases of DNA.

retrosynthesis.about: Retrosynthesis plans a synthesis backwards: start from the target, cut bonds on paper, and work back to compounds you can buy. It is how chemists, and now algorithms, find routes to complex molecules.

catalytic-chemistry.about: Catalysts speed up reactions without being used up. They make most industrial chemicals possible, cut energy use and waste, and decide which product forms when several are possible.

reactive-matter.about: Reactive matter covers the short-lived, high-energy species that drive many reactions: radicals, carbenes, ions and excited molecules. Taming them opens reactions that ordinary chemistry cannot reach.

green-chemistry.about: Green chemistry designs products and processes that use less hazardous material and waste less from the start. It looks at solvents, energy, atom economy and what happens to a product after use.

photochemistry.about: Photochemistry uses light to drive reactions. Absorbed photons create excited molecules that react in ways heat cannot achieve, from photosynthesis to solar fuels and light-driven synthesis.

electrochemistry.about: Electrochemistry studies reactions that move electrons through a circuit. It powers batteries, fuel cells and electrolysers, protects metals from corrosion and offers a clean way to drive synthesis.

inorganic-chemistry.about: Inorganic chemistry covers the whole periodic table beyond carbon: metals, their complexes and solid compounds. It is behind catalysts, pigments, magnets, batteries and metal-based drugs.

industrial-chemistry.about: Industrial chemistry turns laboratory reactions into products made by the tonne. It balances yield, cost, safety and environmental impact across fertilisers, fuels, polymers and fine chemicals.

chemical-engineering.about: Chemical engineering designs the reactors, separations and plants that make chemistry work at scale. It applies transport, thermodynamics and control to run processes safely and efficiently.

quality-control.about: Quality control checks that every batch is what its label says: identity, purity and strength. In pharmaceuticals it is regulated by GMP and pharmacopoeias, and errors can reach patients.

applied-chemistry.about: Applied chemistry takes chemical knowledge into everyday products and problems: agriculture, coatings, cosmetics, water treatment and more. It is where chemistry meets daily life.

forensic-chemistry.about: Forensic chemistry analyses evidence for investigations and courts: drugs, poisons, fibres, residues and fire debris. Its results must be accurate, traceable and able to stand up to cross-examination.

energy-chemistry.about: Energy chemistry develops the materials and reactions behind cleaner power: hydrogen, solar fuels, batteries and carbon capture. It connects molecular design to the energy transition.

food-chemistry.about: Food chemistry studies what food is made of and how it changes when we cook, store or digest it. It covers flavour, nutrition, safety and the additives that keep food fresh.

medicinal-chemistry.about: Medicinal chemistry designs and optimises molecules that become medicines. It links structure to biological activity, balancing potency, safety and how the body absorbs and clears a drug.

biological-chemistry.about: Biological chemistry explains life at the molecular level: how enzymes work, how proteins and DNA interact, and how cells turn food into energy. It is the bridge between chemistry and biology.

drug-discovery.about: Drug discovery is the path from a disease target to a clinical candidate. It combines screening, design and testing to find molecules that are active, safe and able to reach the right place in the body.

bioorganic-chemistry.about: Bioorganic chemistry uses organic chemistry to understand and imitate biology. It studies natural products, how organisms build them, and how to make or modify them in the lab.

polymer-chemistry.about: Polymer chemistry builds giant molecules from small repeating units. Their chain length and structure decide whether you get a rubber, a fibre, a gel or a hard plastic.

marine-chemistry.about: Marine chemistry studies the oceans as a chemical system: seawater composition, nutrient cycles, ocean acidification and the unusual molecules made by marine organisms.

environmental-chemistry.about: Environmental chemistry follows chemicals through air, water and soil: where pollutants come from, how they transform and how to remove them. It underpins environmental regulation and remediation.

computational-chemistry.about: Computational chemistry uses computers to model molecules and reactions, from quantum calculations on a few atoms to simulations of whole proteins. It predicts properties before anything is made.

chemoinformatics.about: Chemoinformatics turns molecules into data that computers can learn from. With descriptors, fingerprints and models it predicts properties and activities, and searches huge chemical libraries.

autonomous-chemistry.about: Autonomous chemistry combines robots and machine learning into self-driving labs. The system chooses the next experiment, runs it, analyses the result and learns, faster than a human loop.

chemical-data-science-and-automation.about: Chemical data science organises, cleans and analyses the data chemistry produces, and automates the steps between experiment and insight. Good data pipelines make every model and decision better.

chemistry-ai-and-ml-applications.about: This field applies machine learning to chemical problems: predicting properties, proposing new molecules, planning syntheses and reading spectra. It is changing how fast chemistry moves.

ai-in-chemistry-real-use-cases.about: Real-world cases where AI is already used in chemistry, in companies and labs: what was done, what it saved, and what did not work. Evidence rather than hype.

the-artificial-intelligence.about: Wider advances in artificial intelligence that matter to science: new models, tools and methods, and what they mean for research, from language models to scientific agents.

nanochemistry.about: Nanochemistry makes and studies materials a few nanometres across, where size changes colour, reactivity and conductivity. It feeds medicine, catalysis, electronics and energy.

chemistry-of-materials.about: Materials chemistry designs solids with useful properties: conducting, magnetic, porous, strong or light-responsive. It connects how atoms are arranged to how a material performs.

sustainable-materials-and-circular-chemi.about: Circular chemistry designs materials that can be reused, recycled or safely returned to nature, and turns waste into feedstock. It aims to keep molecules in use instead of in landfill.

supramolecular-chemistry.about: Supramolecular chemistry is chemistry beyond the bond: molecules holding onto each other through weak forces to self-assemble, recognise partners and build machines.

nuclear-chemistry.about: Nuclear chemistry studies radioactive elements and nuclear reactions. It powers reactors, dates ancient objects and produces the radioisotopes used to image and treat disease.

surface-chemistry.about: Surface chemistry studies what happens at the boundary between phases, where most catalysis, corrosion and adsorption take place. A few atoms at the surface can control a whole material's behaviour.

wisdom-and-stories.about: Reflections and life stories from chemists: how they chose their path, what failed, what they learned, and what they would tell someone starting out.

chemistry-news.about: The main chemistry headlines across all fields: notable discoveries, awards, policy, industry moves and the stories shaping the discipline this week.

the-chemistry.about: The foundations of chemistry explained clearly: atoms, bonds, reactions and the ideas that connect every field, for students and for anyone curious about how matter works.

modern-chemistry.about: What is new in chemistry right now: emerging methods, unexpected results and ideas that change how chemists think about matter and reactions.

creative-chemistry.about: Chemistry seen through art, design and imagination: molecules as visual objects, chemistry in culture, and unconventional ways to explain science.

chemistry-professionals.about: For people building a career in chemistry: jobs, skills, interviews, industry and academic paths, and how chemists move between them.

failed-discoveries-that-changed-science.about: Accidents, mistakes and failed experiments that turned into breakthroughs, from penicillin to Teflon. The stories behind them and what they say about how science really works.

amazing-lab-experiments.about: Striking experiments and demonstrations that make chemistry visible: colour changes, flames, crystals and reactions that show a principle in seconds.

molecular-systems.about: Molecular systems chemistry studies networks of molecules that together show behaviour no single molecule has: replication, motion, memory and the first steps towards life.

chemical-systems.about: Chemical systems covers complex reaction networks, oscillating reactions and chemistry far from equilibrium, where patterns, rhythms and feedback emerge from simple rules.
